\chapter{Ahora, Hoy --- Now and Today}
\label{ch:ahora-hoy}
\hlchaptermodality{252}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can place what I am saying in time.}

I can place what I am saying in time.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ahora · hoy]{ahora · hoy — now and today}

\label{lesson:ES-C65-ahora-hoy}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Mañana} — tomorrow. \emph{La hora} — the hour.

Two more time words, and both are hiding something you already know.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{\textbf{Ahora}} — \emph{now}. Look at what is sitting in the middle of it: \emph{\textbf{hora}}, the word for \emph{hour} you learned long ago.

Latin said \emph{\textbf{hac hora}} — \emph{at this hour}. Two words, worn together into one, and the \emph{h} in the middle went silent along the way. \emph{Now} is literally \textbf{this hour}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{\textbf{Hoy}} — \emph{today}. Latin said \emph{\textbf{hodie}}, which was itself \emph{hoc die}, \emph{this day}.

So the pair is symmetrical, and neither has parts any more: \emph{this hour} wore down to \emph{ahora}, \emph{this day} wore down to three letters. Spanish is full of these — phrases that stopped being phrases.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
And now you can put a time on the tense you learned for the moment:

\begin{quote}
\emph{\textbf{Ahora}} \emph{estoy comiendo.} — Right now, I'm eating. \emph{\textbf{Hoy}} \emph{voy a comer con ella.} — Today I'm going to eat with her.
\end{quote}

Notice which tense each one takes. \emph{Ahora} goes with the progressive, because both mean \emph{at this instant}. \emph{Hoy} covers a whole day, so it takes the ordinary forms — including the going-to future, which is how Spanish says the thing English says with \emph{I'm eating}.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ahora}, \emph{hoy}, \emph{mañana}
  \item \emph{Ahora estoy comiendo}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\emph{Ahora} was which two Latin words? (\emph{\textbf{Hac hora}} — \emph{this hour}.)

And \emph{hoy}? (\emph{\textbf{Hodie}}, which was \emph{this day}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
